abstracts.abstract: We introduce a novel theoretical framework, called Parameterized Analysis of Dynamic Data Structures (PADDS), which fundamentally reconsiders how we model and analyze algorithms operating on evolving inputs. Traditional complexity analysis treats the entire input as a uniform entity, obscuring the structural properties that determine algorithmic performance. Our framework instead characterizes computation through a set of structural parameters that capture intrinsic properties of both the data and the operations applied to it. We establish a new complexity hierarchy that separates problems previously grouped together under classical complexity classes, revealing fine-grained distinctions in computational difficulty. The framework yields unexpected connections between seemingly unrelated areas: dynamic graph connectivity, document streaming, and cache replacement policies all admit unified analysis under PADDS. We prove that this parameterization is intrinsic by demonstrating that any algorithm achieving performance parametrized by our measures must essentially exploit the corresponding structural properties. This work establishes the foundations for a new research direction that bridges parameterized complexity theory with the analysis of sequential and parallel algorithms on dynamic data, offering both new lower bound techniques and algorithmic design principles.

We present a significantly improved analysis of the k-server problem on general metric spaces, achieving a competitive ratio of O(log k log Δ), where Δ denotes the aspect ratio of the metric space, improving upon the long-standing O(k log Δ) bound. Our approach introduces the concept of fractional covering arguments combined with a refined potential function analysis that captures the interaction between server movements more precisely than previous methods. The key innovation lies in a new decomposition technique that allows us to treat the logarithmic factors separately, enabling a modular improvement that can be applied to related online problems. We extend our techniques to obtain improved bounds for the weighted paging problem and the bandwidth allocation problem, demonstrating the broader applicability of our analytic framework. The analysis is significantly simpler than previous approaches achieving comparable bounds, relying only on standard convexity arguments and a novel application of the multiplicative weights update method. We provide a tight lower bound of Ω(log k) for any deterministic algorithm on certain metric spaces, establishing that our result is optimal up to a constant factor in k.

We present GraphFlow, a novel distributed computing system designed for processing large-scale graph streams with complex analytical queries. Unlike existing systems that treat graph processing and stream processing as separate concerns, GraphFlow introduces a unified programming model that naturally expresses queries over both historical graph structure and streaming edge insertions. The system introduces a new data structure called the Temporal Adjacency Forest (TAF), which maintains compact representations of graph evolution while supporting efficient query evaluation. We develop a distributed execution engine that partitions the TAF across multiple machines using a locality-aware scheme that minimizes communication during query processing. The key architectural innovation is a two-phase evaluation strategy: an offline preprocessing phase builds and maintains the TAF, while an online query phase exploits precomputed results to achieve sublinear response times for reachability, pattern matching, and aggregate queries. GraphFlow supports the full expressiveness of Cypher-like graph query languages extended with temporal operators. Our experimental evaluation on graphs with billions of edges demonstrates that GraphFlow achieves order-of-magnitude improvements in query latency over state-of-the-art systems while maintaining high throughput for streaming updates.

We present CachePact, a significantly improved cache management system for modern heterogeneous memory hierarchies that achieves substantial speedups over existing policies. CachePact is based on a principled approach that models cache management as a structured prediction problem, learning to predict cache utility from features derived from memory access patterns, data layout information, and hardware performance counters. The system introduces a novel hierarchical decision framework that makes cache allocation decisions at multiple granularities—page-level, line-level, and set-level—based on learned utility predictions. Our key algorithmic contribution is an efficient online learning algorithm that adapts to changing access patterns without requiring offline training, achieving robust performance across diverse workloads. We implement CachePact in Linux and evaluate it on a range of data-intensive applications including graph analytics, machine learning inference, and scientific computing. Our experiments on real hardware with Intel and AMD processors show that CachePact achieves up to 2.3× speedup over state-of-the-art learned cache policies and 3.1× speedup over traditional LRU, with particularly large improvements for applications with irregular memory access patterns. The system introduces minimal overhead and scales effectively to multi-core configurations.
